titleStmt.title: Action Memorandum From the Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security Affairs (Derwinski) and the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development (McPherson) to Secretary of State Shultz

div.head: 392. Action Memorandum From the Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security Affairs (Derwinski) and the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development (McPherson) to Secretary of State Shultz

list.label: SUBJECT
list.item: ESF for Ecuador After the Earthquake

div.p: Whether to identify $20 to $25 million in FY 1987 ESF to reallocate to Ecuador to help offset the economic effects of the earthquake’s destruction of the oil pipeline.

Coming off a year in which declining oil prices had already seriously affected its fiscal revenues and foreign currency earnings, Ecuador has experienced a series of further economic catastrophes in 1987 including coffee price declines, floods, land slides and, most recent, the earthquake in the eastern part of the country which destroyed the country’s vital oil pipeline. Vice President Bush visited Ecuador following the earthquake and would like to see the United States take the lead in providing additional assistance. The NSC is also interested and has chaired three interagency meetings designed to address the extent of the current financing crisis in Ecuador, identify existing sources of funding, and ascertain the possibilities for additional U.S. assistance. Following the last NSC-chaired meeting, the Department prepared a background paper describing the current financial situation in Ecuador (Tab 1).

In our estimation, Ecuador faces a 1987 balance of payments financing gap of about $1 billion. Potential contributions from international financial institutions, commercial banks and Paris Club official creditors could provide $900 million, leaving about $100 million still unfunded. ARA believes that a U.S. contribution on the order of $30 million would help encourage provision of the remaining amounts from other donors such as the Japanese. (The USG has provided over $30 million in disaster-related assistance, but this did not deal with the balance of payments gap. We have also allocated $12.5 million in FY 1987 ESF to Ecuador, which was programmed before the earthquake and has yet to be obligated. Thus the $30 million would be additional to these amounts.)

In the NSC-chaired meetings, the Department and AID have taken the position that any decisions and recommendations on possible reallocations of existing foreign assistance funds to Ecuador should be made by you. We have discussed the possibility of providing additional PL 480 wheat; however, the Embassy opposes this option and we could also expect difficulties in the interagency process because it would replace likely commercial sales. We will also deobligate some $5 million in the Ecuador DA pipeline and the current year DA budget for reobligation for reconstruction purposes. Deobligation of DA from other countries in the ARA region and reobligation to Ecuador does not seem to be a likely possibility in this case.

The only remaining possibility is thus reallocation of unobligated balances remaining in FY 1987 ESF. Of the $3,550 million in ESF appropriated under the FY 1987 CR, $1,938 million remains unobligated as of April 1. However, of this amount, $1,711 million is either earmarked or in Central America, accounts which enjoy Congressional support. Of the earmarked funds, all but Cyprus ($15 million), Ireland ($35 million) and Uruguay ($12 million) represent our own highest priorities (Egypt, Pakistan, Philippines, etc.). Any effort to use earmarked money for Ecuador would require consultations under Sec. 614 authority. We doubt we could obtain Congressional support to break either Cyprus or Ireland (based on past experience) and any success with Uruguay is also doubtful, given last year’s experience.

The remaining balance is therefore $227 million, as shown in Tab 2. Over 40 percent of the total is in Africa and another 23 percent in moderate Arab states (Jordan, Morocco, Oman, Mideast Regional). All of it has, of course, already been publicly allocated (some of it due to be obligated imminently) and any reductions will have repercussions with the countries concerned. Moreover, we still remain committed to provide $10 million ESF in support of the South Pacific fisheries treaty. Thus the outlook for available ESF is bleak.
Nonetheless, Febres Cordero will be bitterly disappointed if we cannot reciprocate his vigorous and principled support of policies we favor with the emergency ESF he seeks.

The decision, then, is whether the need to help Ecuador is great enough to merit creating problems elsewhere by reallocating money already committed to other countries. If you believe so, we suggest John Whitehead chair a meeting with the regional Assistant Secretaries and ourselves to sort out where the necessary reductions will be made. If you choose not to reallocate FY 1987 ESF for Ecuador, we will so inform the NSC and continue with our efforts to find other sources of assistance. The principal option for non-ESF assistance appears to be limited to PL 480 food aid.
That John Whitehead chair a meeting with the regional Assistant Secretaries and ourselves to determine how much and from where additional FY 1987 ESF will be reallocated to Ecuador.
That we inform the NSC that the ESF situation is too tight to allow for reallocation to Ecuador and that we will therefore continue to seek other sources of additional assistance.

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, George P. Shultz Papers, Box 58C, Ecuador. Confidential. Sent through Whitehead. Drafted on April 16 and revised on April 28 and April 30 by Boyce; cleared by Gelbard and T, AID/PPC, AID/LAC, and EB. A stamped notation at the top of the first page indicates that Shultz saw the memorandum.
No minutes of these meetings have been found.
Attached but not printed is a background paper
Attached but not printed is a paper on the remaining balance.
There is no indication of Shultz’s approval or disapproval of this recommendation.
Shultz indicated his approval by writing his initials, which were dated May 1 by a stamped notation.
